exam_set.title: 令和7年度 基本情報技術者試験 科目B 公開問題
exam_set.description: Practice with Japanese questions, romaji support, English translation, and explanations.

questions.jp:
次のプログラム中の a と b に入れる正しい答えの組合せを，解答群の中から選べ。

関数 function1 が受け取る引数と，関数 function2 が受け取る引数とが同じとき，二つの関数は同じ値を返す。ここで，引数 n と引数 m は正の整数であり，引数 m は引数 n よりも10以上大きい数とする。
questions.romaji:
Tsugi no puroguramu-chuu no a to b ni ireru tadashii kotae no kumiawase o, kaitougun no naka kara erabe.
Kansuu function1 ga uketoru hikisuu to, kansuu function2 ga uketoru hikisuu to ga onaji toki, futatsu no kansuu wa onaji atai o kaesu. Koko de, hikisuu n to hikisuu m wa sei no seisuu de ari, hikisuu m wa hikisuu n yori mo 10 ijou ookii kazu to suru.
questions.en:
Pick the correct combination of answers for blanks a and b in the program below.
When function1 and function2 are given the same arguments, both functions return the same value. Here, n and m are positive integers, and m is at least 10 larger than n.
questions.supplementalHtml:
〔プログラム〕

○整数型: function1(整数型: n, 整数型: m)
  整数型: count ← 0
  整数型: i
  for (i を n から m まで 1 ずつ増やす)
    if ((i mod 4) が 0 と等しい)
      count ← count + 1
    endif
  endfor
  return count

○整数型: function2(整数型: n, 整数型: m)
  整数型: count ← 0
  整数型: tempN ← n
  整数型: i, j
  for (   a   )
    if ((tempN mod 4) が 0 と等しい)
      繰返し処理を終了する
    endif
    tempN ← tempN + 1
  endfor

  for (   b   )
    count ← count + 1
  endfor
  return count

options.label: ア
options.jp: a: i を1から2まで1つ増やす ／ b: j を n から始めて m を超えない範囲で tempN ずつ増やす
options.romaji: a: i o 1 kara 2 made 1 tsu fuyasu / b: j o n kara hajimete m o koenai han'i de tempN zutsu fuyasu
options.en: a: increase i from 1 to 2 by 1 / b: increase j by tempN starting from n within the range not exceeding m

options.label: イ
options.jp: a: i を1から2まで1つ増やす ／ b: j を tempN から m まで1ずつ増やす
options.romaji: a: i o 1 kara 2 made 1 tsu fuyasu / b: j o tempN kara m made 1 zutsu fuyasu
options.en: a: increase i from 1 to 2 by 1 / b: increase j from tempN to m by 1

options.label: ウ
options.jp: a: i を1から2まで1つ増やす ／ b: j を tempN から始めて m を超えない範囲で4ずつ増やす
options.romaji: a: i o 1 kara 2 made 1 tsu fuyasu / b: j o tempN kara hajimete m o koenai han'i de 4 zutsu fuyasu
options.en: a: increase i from 1 to 2 by 1 / b: increase j by 4 starting from tempN within the range not exceeding m

options.label: エ
options.jp: a: i を1から3まで1つ増やす ／ b: j を n から始めて m を超えない範囲で tempN ずつ増やす
options.romaji: a: i o 1 kara 3 made 1 tsu fuyasu / b: j o n kara hajimete m o koenai han'i de tempN zutsu fuyasu
options.en: a: increase i from 1 to 3 by 1 / b: increase j by tempN starting from n within the range not exceeding m

options.label: オ
options.jp: a: i を1から3まで1つ増やす ／ b: j を tempN から m まで1ずつ増やす
options.romaji: a: i o 1 kara 3 made 1 tsu fuyasu / b: j o tempN kara m made 1 zutsu fuyasu
options.en: a: increase i from 1 to 3 by 1 / b: increase j from tempN to m by 1

options.label: カ
options.jp: a: i を1から3まで1つ増やす ／ b: j を tempN から始めて m を超えない範囲で4ずつ増やす
options.romaji: a: i o 1 kara 3 made 1 tsu fuyasu / b: j o tempN kara hajimete m o koenai han'i de 4 zutsu fuyasu
options.en: a: increase i from 1 to 3 by 1 / b: increase j by 4 starting from tempN within the range not exceeding m

questions.explanation:
ELI5:
Imagine you have two workers counting how many multiples of 4 exist between two numbers n and m. Worker 1 (function1) walks every single number from n to m one by one and raises his hand every time he hits a multiple of 4. Worker 2 (function2) works in two stages. First, he takes small steps forward from n until he lands on the nearest multiple of 4. Then he jumps exactly 4 steps at a time from there and counts each landing. Both workers end up with the same total count.
Now look at the wrong options. Option a has the first loop capped at 2 iterations and the second loop stepping by tempN, making both parts wrong. Option i has the first loop capped at 2 and the second loop stepping by 1, which counts every integer from tempN to m instead of only multiples of 4. Option u has the second loop correctly stepping by 4 from tempN but the first loop capped at 2, which fails when n mod 4 = 1 because 3 steps are needed. Option e has the first loop correctly running up to 3 but the second loop starts from n instead of tempN and steps by tempN. Option o has the first loop correctly running up to 3 but the second loop steps by 1, overcounting every integer instead of jumping between multiples of 4.

Technical breakdown:
function1 iterates i from n to m inclusive and increments count whenever i mod 4 = 0. It directly counts all multiples of 4 in the range n to m.
function2 achieves the same result in two phases.
Phase 1 is blank a. tempN starts at n. The loop checks whether tempN mod 4 = 0 on each iteration and breaks immediately if true. If not, tempN is incremented by 1 and the loop continues. This finds the first multiple of 4 that is greater than or equal to n. The maximum number of iterations needed depends on n mod 4. If n mod 4 = 0, the condition is true immediately. If n mod 4 = 3, one increment is needed. If n mod 4 = 2, two increments are needed. If n mod 4 = 1, three increments are needed. Therefore the loop must run up to 3 times. Capping at 2 fails the n mod 4 = 1 case, leaving tempN at a value that is not a multiple of 4.
Phase 2 is blank b. Starting from tempN, which is now guaranteed to be the first multiple of 4 greater than or equal to n, the loop steps by 4 each iteration without exceeding m, and increments count by 1 each time. Since consecutive multiples of 4 are always exactly 4 apart, stepping by 4 from the first one lands on every subsequent multiple of 4 up to m with no misses and no overcounting. This matches exactly what function1 counted.

Wrong answer analysis:
a -- Both a and b are wrong. The first loop capped at 2 fails when n mod 4 = 1. The second loop stepping by tempN uses a variable step size that does not reliably land on multiples of 4. A student who does not trace through the worst case for phase 1 and does not think carefully about what step size the second loop needs will be drawn to this option.
i -- The first loop capped at 2 is wrong for the same reason as option a. The second loop starts at tempN which looks correct, but stepping by 1 means it counts every integer from tempN to m instead of only multiples of 4. This is a particularly dangerous trap because the starting point of the second loop is right but the step size is wrong. A student who correctly identifies that the second loop should start at tempN but does not think about the step size will select this option.
u -- The second loop is fully correct, stepping by 4 from tempN up to m. The only error is the first loop capped at 2. A student who verifies the second loop first and finds it correct may then select this option without checking whether 2 iterations are always enough for the first loop. Testing n mod 4 = 1 reveals the failure.
e -- The first loop running up to 3 is correct. But the second loop starts from n instead of tempN and steps by tempN. Starting from n instead of tempN means the second loop does not begin at a guaranteed multiple of 4. Stepping by tempN uses a variable that has already been modified by phase 1 and does not represent a fixed interval of 4. A student who correctly solves blank a but then misreads the second loop options will land here.
o -- The first loop running up to 3 is correct. But the second loop steps by 1, counting every integer from tempN to m instead of jumping between multiples of 4. A student who correctly solves blank a but does not reason about what step size the second loop needs will select this option.

Correct answer: カ

questions.jp:
次のプログラム中の □ に入れる正しい答えを，解答群の中から選べ。

関数 change は，10より大きい整数を引数 n で受け取り，1円玉，5円玉，10円玉を使ってちょうど n 円にする組合せの総数を返す。

例えば，12円にする組合せは，次のように数えられる。10円玉を使わない場合には，1円玉と5円玉だけでちょうど12円にすることになる。その組合せは，使える5円玉の枚数が0以上(12÷5の商)以下なので，(12÷5の商)＋1＝3通りある。同様に，10円玉を1枚使う場合には，1円玉と5円玉だけでちょうど2円にすることになり，その組合せは(2÷5の商)＋1＝1通りある。10円玉を2枚以上使う組合せはない。よって，1円玉，5円玉，10円玉を使ってちょうど12円にする組合せは，3＋1＝4通りである。
questions.romaji:
Tsugi no puroguramu-chuu no shikaku ni ireru tadashii kotae o, kaitougun no naka kara erabe.
Kansuu change wa, 10 yori ookii seisuu o hikisuu n de uketori, 1-en-dama, 5-en-dama, 10-en-dama o tsukatte choudo n-en ni suru kumiawase no sousuu o kaesu.
Tatoeba, 12-en ni suru kumiawase wa, tsugi no you ni kazoerareru. 10-en-dama o tsukawanai baai ni wa, 1-en-dama to 5-en-dama dake de choudo 12-en ni suru koto ni naru. Sono kumiawase wa, tsukaeru 5-en-dama no maisuu ga 0 ijou (12÷5 no shou) ika nano de, (12÷5 no shou)＋1＝3 toori aru. Douyou ni, 10-en-dama o 1-mai tsukau baai ni wa, 1-en-dama to 5-en-dama dake de choudo 2-en ni suru koto ni nari, sono kumiawase wa (2÷5 no shou)＋1＝1 toori aru. 10-en-dama o 2-mai ijou tsukau kumiawase wa nai. Yotte, 1-en-dama, 5-en-dama, 10-en-dama o tsukatte choudo 12-en ni suru kumiawase wa, 3＋1＝4 toori de aru.
questions.en:
Pick the correct answer for the blank in the program below.
The function change takes an integer n greater than 10 and returns the total number of ways to make exactly n yen using 1-yen, 5-yen, and 10-yen coins.
For example, count the ways to make 12 yen like this. Using no 10-yen coin, you make 12 yen with only 1-yen and 5-yen coins; the number of 5-yen coins ranges from 0 to floor(12/5), giving floor(12/5)+1 = 3 ways. Using one 10-yen coin, you make the remaining 2 yen with 1-yen and 5-yen coins, giving floor(2/5)+1 = 1 way. There is no way to use two or more 10-yen coins. So the total number of ways to make exactly 12 yen is 3+1 = 4.
questions.supplementalHtml:
〔プログラム〕

○整数型: change(整数型: n)
  整数型: count ← 0
  整数型: rest ← n
  while (   □   )
    count ← count + (rest ÷ 5 の商) + 1
    rest ← rest − 10
  endwhile
  return count
questions.explanation:
ELI5:
Imagine you have a pile of coins worth n yen and you want to count how many different ways you can make exactly n yen using 1 yen coins, 5 yen coins, and 10 yen coins. The function works by peeling off one 10 yen coin at a time. Each time you remove a 10 yen coin from the pile, you count how many ways you can make the remaining amount using only 1 yen and 5 yen coins. The number of ways to make any amount using only 1 yen and 5 yen coins is simply how many 5 yen coins you can fit in, plus 1. For example if you have 12 yen left, you can use zero, one, or two 5 yen coins, giving 3 ways. The while loop keeps removing 10 yen coins one at a time and adding up the combinations for each remaining amount, until there are not enough coins left to remove another 10 yen coin.
Now look at the wrong options. Option i says rest >= 5, which stops the loop too early, missing remainders below 5 that still contribute valid combinations. Option u says rest >= 10, which stops the loop when rest drops below 10, missing the final iteration where the remainder is between 0 and 9. Option e says rest > 0, which misses the case where rest equals exactly 0, which contributes 1 valid combination. Option o says rest > 5, which stops the loop when rest is 5 or below, missing remainders from 0 to 5. Option ka says rest > 10, which stops the loop when rest is 10 or below, cutting off even more valid iterations.

Technical breakdown:
The function change takes a positive integer n greater than 10 and returns the total number of ways to make exactly n yen using 1 yen, 5 yen, and 10 yen coins.
The algorithm works by iterating over the number of 10 yen coins used, from zero upward. rest starts at n and decreases by 10 on each iteration, representing the remaining amount after removing one more 10 yen coin. On each iteration, count is increased by (rest divided by 5, integer division) plus 1, which is the number of ways to make rest yen using only 1 yen and 5 yen coins. If rest yen is available and you can use zero, one, two, or up to floor(rest divided by 5) five yen coins, each choice uniquely determines how many 1 yen coins are needed, giving exactly floor(rest divided by 5) plus 1 combinations.
The while loop must continue as long as rest is greater than or equal to 0, because even a remainder of 0 contributes exactly 1 valid combination (using zero 5 yen coins and zero 1 yen coins). After the count update, rest is decremented by 10, which will eventually make rest negative, correctly terminating the loop.
Tracing with n = 12: rest = 12, 12 >= 0 is true, count += (12 div 5) + 1 = 3, rest becomes 2. rest = 2, 2 >= 0 is true, count += (2 div 5) + 1 = 1, rest becomes -8. rest = -8, -8 >= 0 is false, loop ends. count = 4. This matches the expected answer of 4.
Tracing with n = 20: rest = 20, count += (20 div 5) + 1 = 5, rest = 10. rest = 10, count += (10 div 5) + 1 = 3, rest = 0. rest = 0, count += (0 div 5) + 1 = 1, rest = -10. rest = -10, loop ends. count = 9. This is correct for 20 yen.

Wrong answer analysis:
イ -- rest >= 5 stops the loop when rest drops below 5. For n = 12, rest goes 12 then 2, and since 2 >= 5 is false the loop stops after one iteration giving count = 3 instead of 4. This misses all remainders below 5 that still contribute valid combinations. A student who thinks the loop should only continue while at least one 5 yen coin can fit will select this option.
ウ -- rest >= 10 stops the loop when rest drops below 10, meaning the final remainder between 0 and 9 is never processed. For n = 12, only the rest = 12 iteration runs, giving count = 3 instead of 4. A student who thinks the loop should only run while a full 10 yen coin can still be removed will pick this, confusing the loop condition with the subtraction that happens inside the loop.
エ -- rest > 0 correctly handles most cases but fails when rest equals exactly 0. For any n that is an exact multiple of 10, the final remainder after all subtractions is 0, which contributes 1 valid combination (using no 5 yen coins and no 1 yen coins). This option misses that final count. A student who treats 0 remaining yen as meaning no combinations are possible will select this.
オ -- rest > 5 stops the loop when rest is 5 or below, missing remainders from 0 to 5 which all contribute at least 1 valid combination. This is a stricter cutoff than option i and misses more valid iterations.
カ -- rest > 10 stops the loop when rest is 10 or below, which is the most aggressive early cutoff. It misses all remainders from 0 to 10 and produces the most undercounted result of all wrong options.

Correct answer: ア

questions.jp:
次のプログラム中の a と b に入れる正しい答えの組合せを，解答群の中から選べ。ここで，配列の要素番号は1から始まる。

関数 push は，引数で与えられた整数をスタックに格納する。格納できた場合は true を返し，格納できなかった場合は false を返す。

関数 pop は，スタックから値を取り出して返す。スタックが空のときは未定義の値を返す。

スタックを，要素数が4である大域の整数型の配列 stack 及び次に値を格納する位置を示す大域の変数 stackPos で表現する。スタックの初期状態を図に示す。プログラムでは，配列の領域外を参照してはならないものとする。
questions.romaji:
Tsugi no puroguramu-chuu no a to b ni ireru tadashii kotae no kumiawase o, kaitougun no naka kara erabe. Koko de, hairetsu no youso bangou wa 1 kara hajimaru.
Kansuu push wa, hikisuu de ataerareta seisuu o sutakku ni kakunou suru. Kakunou dekita baai wa true o kaeshi, kakunou dekinakatta baai wa false o kaesu.
Kansuu pop wa, sutakku kara atai o toridashite kaesu. Sutakku ga kara no toki wa miteigi no atai o kaesu.
Sutakku o, yousosuu ga 4 de aru taiiki no seisuu-gata no hairetsu stack oyobi tsugi ni atai o kakunou suru ichi o shimesu taiiki no hensuu stackPos de hyougen suru. Sutakku no shoki joutai o zu ni shimesu. Puroguramu de wa, hairetsu no ryouiki-gai o sanshou shite wa naranai mono to suru.
questions.en:
Choose the correct combination of answers for blanks a and b in the program below. Array index numbers start at 1.
The function push stores the integer argument onto a stack. It returns true if it could store the value, and false if it could not.
The function pop takes a value off the stack and returns it. If the stack is empty, it returns an undefined value.
The stack is represented by a global 4-element integer array stack and a global variable stackPos that points to the position where the next value will be stored. The figure shows the stack's initial state. The program must never reference outside the array bounds.
questions.supplementalHtml:
図 スタックの初期状態

要素番号1234
stack43（未定義）（未定義）

注記: 網掛けはその要素が未定義であることを示す。stackPos は要素番号3を指す。

〔プログラム〕

大域: 整数型: stackPos ← 3
大域: 整数型の配列: stack ← {4, 3, 未定義の値, 未定義の値}

○論理型: push(整数型: inputData)
  if (stackPos ≦ stack の要素数)
    stack[   a   ] ← inputData
    stackPos ← stackPos + 1
    return true
  else
    return false
  endif

○整数型: pop()
  整数型: popData ← 未定義の値
  if (stackPos > 1)
    stackPos ←   b
    popData ← stack[stackPos]
    stack[stackPos] ← 未定義の値
  endif
  return popData
questions.explanation:
ELI5:
Imagine a stack of plates where each plate has a number written on it. The stack can hold at most 4 plates. A pointer called stackPos always points to the position where the next plate will go. At the start, stackPos is 3, meaning positions 1 and 2 already have plates (with values 4 and 3) and the next plate will go into position 3.
The push function adds a plate. It checks whether stackPos is still within the stack size, writes the new value at position stackPos, then moves the pointer one step forward to prepare for the next addition.
The pop function removes the top plate. It checks whether the stack has anything to remove, moves the pointer one step backward to the last filled position, reads the value there, then clears that position.
For blank a in push: stackPos currently points to where the next item goes, so you write inputData into stack[stackPos], then increment stackPos. So a = stackPos.
For blank b in pop: stackPos currently points to the next empty position, so the last filled item is one position before it. You must move stackPos back by 1 first, then read stack[stackPos]. So b = stackPos minus 1.
Now look at the wrong options. Option a has a = stackPos and b = stackPos + 1, which moves the pointer forward during pop instead of backward, reading an undefined position. Option u has a = stackPos minus 1 and b = stackPos + 1, which writes to the wrong position during push and moves forward during pop. Option e has a = stackPos minus 1 and b = stackPos minus 1, which writes to the wrong position during push even though pop is handled correctly.

Technical breakdown:
The stack is implemented using a fixed-size integer array called stack with 4 elements indexed from 1, and a global variable stackPos that indicates the next available position for writing. This is a standard top-of-stack pointer convention where stackPos points one position ahead of the last written element.
At initialization stackPos is 3, stack[1] = 4, stack[2] = 3, and stack[3] and stack[4] are undefined. This confirms that positions 1 and 2 are filled and stackPos points to the next empty slot.
For the push function: the condition checks stackPos <= stack size (4), meaning there is still room. The write must happen at stack[stackPos] because that is the next available position. After writing, stackPos is incremented by 1 to advance the pointer. Therefore blank a = stackPos. Writing to stackPos minus 1 would overwrite the last pushed value rather than filling the next empty slot, which is wrong.
For the pop function: the condition checks stackPos > 1, meaning the stack is not empty. Since stackPos points to the next empty position, the last filled position is stackPos minus 1. The pointer must first be decremented to stackPos minus 1, then the value at that position is read into popData, and that position is cleared. Therefore blank b = stackPos minus 1. Setting b = stackPos + 1 would move the pointer further forward into undefined territory and then read from an unwritten position.
Tracing push with inputData = 5: stackPos = 3, 3 <= 4 so proceed. stack[3] = 5. stackPos becomes 4. Stack is now {4, 3, 5, undefined}. Correct.
Tracing pop: stackPos = 4, 4 > 1 so proceed. stackPos becomes 3. popData = stack[3] = 5. stack[3] = undefined. stackPos is back to 3. Correct.

Wrong answer analysis:
a -- a = stackPos is correct for push, but b = stackPos + 1 increments the pointer further forward during pop instead of backward. This makes pop read from an undefined position beyond the last filled element and leaves the stack pointer in an inconsistent state. A student who confuses the direction of pointer movement during pop, thinking pop should advance rather than retreat, will select this option.
u -- a = stackPos minus 1 writes to the position before the current pointer during push, overwriting the most recently pushed value instead of filling the next empty slot. b = stackPos + 1 then compounds the error by moving the pointer forward during pop. Both operations are wrong. A student who misreads the pointer convention and thinks stackPos points to the last filled position rather than the next empty position will be drawn to this option.
e -- a = stackPos minus 1 makes the same push error as option u, writing to the wrong position. b = stackPos minus 1 is actually the correct pop behavior. A student who correctly works out the pop logic but misreads the push logic will land on this option. This is a particularly tricky trap because half the answer is right.

Correct answer: イ

questions.jp:
次の記述中の □ に入れる正しい答えを，解答群の中から選べ。ここで，配列の要素番号は1から始まる。

関数 search は，二つの文字型の配列を，それぞれ引数 data 及び key で受け取り，data から，key の要素の並びと同じ並びを全て探し，その先頭の要素番号を全て格納した配列を返す。見つからなければ，要素数0の配列を返す。

関数 search を search({"a", "b", "a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "c"}, {"a", "b", "c"}) として呼び出すと，/*** β ***/ の行の条件式が真となる回数は □ 回である。
questions.romaji:
Tsugi no kijutsu-chuu no shikaku ni ireru tadashii kotae o, kaitougun no naka kara erabe. Koko de, hairetsu no youso bangou wa 1 kara hajimaru.
Kansuu search wa, futatsu no mojigata no hairetsu o, sorezore hikisuu data oyobi key de uketori, data kara, key no youso no narabi to onaji narabi o subete sagashi, sono sentou no youso bangou o subete kakunou shita hairetsu o kaesu. Mitsukaranakereba, yousosuu 0 no hairetsu o kaesu.
Kansuu search o search({"a", "b", "a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "c"}, {"a", "b", "c"}) to shite yobidasu to, /*** β ***/ no gyou no jouken-shiki ga shin to naru kaisuu wa shikaku kai de aru.
questions.en:
Pick the correct answer for the blank in the description below. Array index numbers start at 1.
The function search takes two character arrays as the arguments data and key. It finds, within data, every place where the same sequence as key appears, and returns an array holding all the starting index numbers. If there is no match, it returns a zero-length array.
When search is called as search({"a", "b", "a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "c"}, {"a", "b", "c"}), the number of times the condition on the line marked /*** β ***/ evaluates to true is □ times.
questions.supplementalHtml:
〔プログラム〕

/* key は，要素数1以上の配列である */
○整数型の配列: search(文字型の配列: data, 文字型の配列: key)
  整数型: i, j, lenData, lenKey
  整数型の配列: result ← {}  // 要素数0の配列

  lenData ← data の要素数
  lenKey ← key の要素数

  /* (lenData − lenKey + 1) が0以下のときは繰返し処理を実行しない */
  for (i を 1 から (lenData − lenKey + 1) まで 1 ずつ増やす)
    for (j を 1 から lenKey まで 1 ずつ増やす)  // α
      if (data[i + j − 1] が key[j] と等しい)  /*** β ***/
        if (j が lenKey と等しい)
          result の末尾に i の値 を追加する
        endif
      else
        α の行から始まる繰返し処理を終了する
      endif
    endfor
  endfor
  return result
questions.explanation:
ELI5:
Imagine you have a long string of letters: a, b, a, b, c, a, b, c. You are looking for a pattern: a, b, c. The function slides the pattern along the string from left to right, checking each position to see if the pattern fits. At each starting position, it compares the letters one by one. The moment a letter does not match, it gives up on that position and moves on. If all letters match, it records the starting position as a hit.
The question asks how many times the comparison at the beta line is true, meaning how many individual letter comparisons succeed across all starting positions.
Starting at position 1: a matches a (true), b matches b (true), a does not match c (false, stop). Two true comparisons.
Starting at position 2: b does not match a (false, stop). Zero true comparisons.
Starting at position 3: a matches a (true), b matches b (true), c matches c (true). Three true comparisons. Hit recorded.
Starting at position 4: b does not match a (false, stop). Zero true comparisons.
Starting at position 5: c does not match a (false, stop). Zero true comparisons.
Starting at position 6: a matches a (true), b matches b (true), c matches c (true). Three true comparisons. Hit recorded.
Total true comparisons: 2 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 3 = 8.

Technical breakdown:
The function search takes two string arrays data and key and returns an array of all starting positions in data where the sequence key appears in full.
lenData = 8, lenKey = 3. The outer loop runs i from 1 to lenData minus lenKey plus 1 = 6, covering all positions where key could possibly start without running off the end of data.
The inner loop runs j from 1 to lenKey = 3. On each iteration it checks whether data[i + j - 1] equals key[j]. This is the beta condition. If it is false, the inner loop breaks immediately via the alpha label. If j reaches lenKey and all comparisons were true, i is appended to result.
Counting true evaluations of the beta condition:
i=1: j=1 data[1]="a" == key[1]="a" true. j=2 data[2]="b" == key[2]="b" true. j=3 data[3]="a" == key[3]="c" false, break. True count: 2.
i=2: j=1 data[2]="b" == key[1]="a" false, break. True count: 0.
i=3: j=1 data[3]="a" == key[1]="a" true. j=2 data[4]="b" == key[2]="b" true. j=3 data[5]="c" == key[3]="c" true, j equals lenKey so record i=3. True count: 3.
i=4: j=1 data[4]="b" == key[1]="a" false, break. True count: 0.
i=5: j=1 data[5]="c" == key[1]="a" false, break. True count: 0.
i=6: j=1 data[6]="a" == key[1]="a" true. j=2 data[7]="b" == key[2]="b" true. j=3 data[8]="c" == key[3]="c" true, j equals lenKey so record i=6. True count: 3.
Total: 2 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 3 = 8.

Wrong answer analysis:
a (1) -- A student who only counts the number of successful full matches would get 2, since the pattern is found at positions 3 and 6. This confuses counting matches with counting true evaluations of the beta condition.
i (2) -- A student who counts only the outer loop iterations where at least one true comparison occurs would get 3 (i=1, i=3, i=6), then adds something incorrectly to reach 2. This reflects partial tracing without tracking each individual j iteration.
u (3) -- A student who counts only the first comparison across all 6 outer iterations without tracing the inner loop would get a small number like 3 (the three starting positions where j=1 is true). Arriving at exactly 3 reflects this shallow trace.
e (4) -- A student who counts total inner loop iterations executed regardless of true or false would count 3+1+3+1+1+3 = 12, then subtract something incorrectly or miscount to reach 4.
o (5) -- A student who counts only the positions where the pattern fully matches (2 matches) and then adds the first partial match at i=1 (2 true comparisons) might reach 2+3=5 through confused arithmetic.
ka (6) -- A student who counts total outer iterations (6) is ignoring the inner loop entirely and just counting how many starting positions were checked.
ki (7) -- A student who counts total inner loop evaluations regardless of outcome: i=1 runs 3 times, i=2 runs 1 time, i=3 runs 3 times, i=4 runs 1 time, i=5 runs 1 time, i=6 runs 3 times = 12 total, then subtracts the 4 false evaluations to get 8. A student who makes an arithmetic error in this approach might get 7.
ku (8) -- This is the correct count as traced above.
ke (9) -- A student who counts total inner loop evaluations without subtracting false ones gets 3+1+3+1+1+3 = 12, then makes a miscalculation and arrives at 9.
ko (10) -- A student who counts total inner loop evaluations regardless of outcome gets 3+1+3+1+1+3 = 12, then subtracts 2 (the number of full matches) to get 10.

Correct answer: ク

questions.en:
Choose the correct combination of answers for blanks a and b in the description below. Array index numbers start at 1.
The "theoretical frequency" is the expected number of people under the assumption that catching disease X is independent of whether a person was vaccinated, derived from aggregated survey data on the vaccine's preventive effect against disease X. Table 1 shows a sample of the aggregated results, and Table 2 shows the theoretical frequencies computed from Table 1.
The function f returns the theoretical frequencies computed from the aggregated results passed in data. The argument and return value are two-dimensional arrays whose rows map to the table rows and whose columns map to the table columns. Each cell is (sum of that row) × (sum of that column) ÷ (grand total).

〔プログラム〕

○実数型の二次元配列: f(実数型の二次元配列: data)
  実数型: t ← data の要素の和
  整数型: row ← data の行数
  整数型: col ← data の列数

                      (data の列番号 c の要素の和) ÷ t
    endfor
  endfor
  return result
questions.explanation:
ELI5:
Imagine you are a scientist trying to figure out whether a vaccine actually works. You collected real data on 154 people showing who got vaccinated and who caught disease X. But to test whether the vaccine made any difference, you first need to calculate what the numbers would look like if the vaccine had absolutely no effect at all. These calculated numbers are called theoretical frequencies.
The idea is simple. If the vaccine does nothing, then the proportion of people who get sick should be the same whether they were vaccinated or not. So for any cell in the table, you calculate its theoretical value by multiplying the total for that row by the total for that column, then dividing by the grand total. This spreads the sick and healthy people proportionally across vaccinated and unvaccinated groups as if the vaccine did not exist.
For blank a, which is the theoretical number of vaccinated people who did not get sick: the vaccinated row total is 88, the did-not-get-sick column total is 140, and the grand total is 154. So a = 88 times 140 divided by 154 = 80.
For blank b, which is the theoretical number of unvaccinated people who got sick: the unvaccinated row total is 66, the got-sick column total is 14, and the grand total is 154. So b = 66 times 14 divided by 154 = 6.

Technical breakdown:
The function f takes a 2D array data representing an observed frequency table and returns a 2D array of the same dimensions containing the theoretical frequencies under the assumption of independence between rows and columns.
The formula applied to each cell is: result[r, c] = (sum of row r) times (sum of column c) divided by t, where t is the grand total of all elements in data.
This formula comes from the chi-squared test of independence in statistics. Under the null hypothesis that the row variable (vaccination status) and the column variable (disease outcome) are independent, the expected count for any cell is the product of its marginal totals divided by the grand total.
Calculating from Table 1:
Row 1 sum (vaccinated): 82 + 6 = 88.
Row 2 sum (unvaccinated): 58 + 8 = 66.
Column 1 sum (did not get sick): 82 + 58 = 140.
Column 2 sum (got sick): 6 + 8 = 14.
Grand total t: 88 + 66 = 154.
Blank a = result[1,1] = 88 times 140 divided by 154 = 12320 divided by 154 = 80.
Blank b = result[2,2] = 66 times 14 divided by 154 = 924 divided by 154 = 6.
The correct combination is a = 80 and b = 6.

Wrong answer analysis:
a (44, 33) -- A student who divides each cell value by 2 or applies some averaging operation rather than the row-times-column-over-total formula will get values in this range. This reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of what theoretical frequency means.
i (58, 8) -- These are the actual observed values from row 2 of Table 1. A student who copies the unvaccinated row directly instead of computing theoretical values will land here. This confuses observed frequency with theoretical frequency.
u (70, 7) -- A student who averages the two row totals or averages column values and divides incorrectly may arrive near these numbers. The values do not follow from any standard formula applied correctly.
e (75, 2) -- A student who uses the correct formula but makes an arithmetic error, or who uses a wrong formula such as row sum plus column sum divided by 2, may reach values near 75. The b value of 2 suggests a student who subtracts something incorrectly from the got-sick column.
o (80, 6) -- A student who correctly computes a = 80 but pairs it with b = 6 has the right values but this option does not exist in the answer table. This is a distractor for students who reach the right numbers but misread the option table.
ka (80, 6) -- This is the correct answer as derived above. a = 80 and b = 6.
ki (82, 6) -- A student who uses the observed value for a (copying 82 directly from Table 1) but correctly computes b = 6 will land here. This is a trap because b is correct but a is the raw observed cell value rather than the theoretical frequency.

Correct answer: カ

questions.supplementalHtml:
図1 A社のファイルサーバの運用

  • ファイルサーバは本社と工場のサーバルームに設置している。
  • ファイルサーバは，磁気テープを使用してファイルのバックアップを取得している。
  • 土曜日の午前2時からフルバックアップを取得し，翌週の火曜日と木曜日の午前2時から増分バックアップを取得している。
  • 情報システム部の担当者は毎週月曜日，火曜日，木曜日の朝10時頃，バックアップジョブの実行結果の確認と磁気テープの交換を行い，磁気テープは耐火金庫に保管している。
  • 磁気テープには上書きモードでバックアップを取得し，1か月分の磁気テープを世代管理している。
  • これまで，フルバックアップからのリストアには平均して4時間，1回の増分バックアップからは平均して0.25時間掛かっている。
  • A社はICT継続のための試験を実施しており，ファイルサーバも試験対象である。

注記 事業影響度分析の結果に基づき，ファイルサーバは，72時間の目標復旧時点（RPO）と120時間の目標復旧時間（RTO）が要求事項として定められている。

questions.explanation:
ELI5:
Imagine a company backs up its files like taking snapshots. Every Saturday at 2am they take a complete snapshot of everything. Then every Tuesday and Thursday at 2am they take a smaller snapshot of only what changed since Saturday. These snapshots are stored on magnetic tapes in a fireproof safe.
The company has two recovery rules. First, if something breaks, the data they recover must be no older than 72 hours before the breakdown. This is called the recovery point objective. Second, the actual recovery process must finish within 120 hours. This is called the recovery time objective.
For blank a1, if a failure happens on Friday at noon, 72 hours before that is Tuesday at noon. So the company must be able to restore data up to at least Tuesday noon. The answer is Tuesday noon, because that is the oldest acceptable recovery point.
For blank a2, if a failure happens on Thursday at noon with all data lost, the restore process needs the Saturday full backup (4 hours) plus the Tuesday incremental backup (0.25 hours) plus the Thursday 2am incremental backup (0.25 hours), totaling 4.5 hours.
For blank a3, under ISMS standards, ICT continuity plans must be approved by top management. The CISO is the highest information security officer in the company, which is top management, so the CISO approves the plan.

Technical breakdown:
Blank a1 relates to RPO (Recovery Point Objective), which is set at 72 hours. RPO defines the maximum acceptable age of data that must be recoverable after a failure. If a failure occurs on Friday at noon, subtracting 72 hours gives Tuesday at noon as the earliest acceptable recovery point. This means the company must be able to restore data that was current as of at least Tuesday noon. The Thursday 2am incremental backup satisfies this requirement since it is more recent than Tuesday noon, but the question asks for the minimum point that must be guaranteed recoverable, which is Tuesday noon (火曜日の正午).
Blank a2 relates to RTO (Recovery Time Objective), which is set at 120 hours. The question asks how long a full restore would actually take if failure occurs Thursday noon. The restore procedure requires first restoring the most recent full backup taken on Saturday at 2am (4 hours), then applying the Tuesday 2am incremental backup (0.25 hours), then applying the Thursday 2am incremental backup (0.25 hours). The Thursday 2am backup was already completed before the Thursday noon failure. Total restore time = 4 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 4.50 hours. This is well within the 120 hour RTO.
Blank a3 relates to governance requirements under JIS Q 27001:2023. ICT continuity planning is a top management responsibility under ISMS. The plan must be authorized by an executive with the authority to commit organizational resources and policy. The CISO (最高情報セキュリティ責任者) holds this role at Company A and is the correct approver. The information systems department staff member is an operational role without authority to approve continuity plans. The internal audit manager conducts audits and evaluates compliance but does not approve the plans being audited, as this would be a conflict of independence.

Wrong answer analysis:
a (月曜日の正午, 4.25, CISO) -- a1 is wrong. Monday noon is 96 hours before Friday noon, which exceeds the 72 hour RPO. Restoring to Monday noon would mean losing more than 72 hours of data, violating the requirement. a2 = 4.25 reflects restoring only the full backup plus one incremental (4 + 0.25), missing the Thursday 2am incremental. A student who forgets that the Thursday incremental was already completed before the noon failure will make this error.
i (月曜日の正午, 4.25, 情報システム部の担当者) -- Same a1 and a2 errors as option a, with the additional error of selecting the information systems staff member as approver. Operational staff do not have the authority to approve ICT continuity plans under ISMS governance requirements.
u (月曜日の正午, 4.25, 内部監査室長) -- The internal audit manager evaluates whether plans comply with standards but must remain independent of the plans themselves. Approving the plan would compromise that independence. This option also carries the wrong a1 and a2 values.
e (月曜日の正午, 4.50, CISO) -- a1 is wrong for the same RPO reason. a2 = 4.50 is correct. a3 = CISO is correct. A student who gets the restore time and approver right but miscalculates the RPO cutoff will land here.
o (月曜日の正午, 4.50, 情報システム部の担当者) -- a1 wrong, a2 correct, a3 wrong. Same RPO error combined with selecting the wrong approver.
ka (火曜日の正午, 4.25, 情報システム部の担当者) -- a1 is correct. a2 = 4.25 reflects missing the Thursday incremental in the restore calculation. a3 is wrong. A student who correctly identifies Tuesday noon as the RPO boundary but forgets the Thursday backup and picks the wrong approver will land here.
ki (火曜日の正午, 4.25, 内部監査室長) -- a1 correct, a2 missing the Thursday incremental, a3 selects the audit manager who cannot approve what they audit.
ku (火曜日の正午, 4.50, CISO) -- All three values are correct. This is the correct answer.
ke (火曜日の正午, 4.50, 情報システム部の担当者) -- a1 and a2 are correct but a3 is wrong. A student who correctly works through the RPO and restore time calculations but does not know that ISMS governance requires executive approval will select the operational staff member.
ko (火曜日の正午, 4.50, 内部監査室長) -- a1 and a2 correct but a3 selects the internal audit manager, which violates audit independence principles.

Correct answer: ク
